DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93, Module 2.

Terminal objective

1.0 Given an engineering print, READ and INTERPRET facility engineering Piping and Instrument Drawings. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.vii

Enabling objectives

1.1 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for the following types of valves: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.vii

  • a. Globe valve
  • b. Gate valve
  • c. Ball valve
  • d. Check valve
  • e. Stop check valve
  • f. Butterfly valve
  • g. Relief valve
  • h. Rupture disk
  • i. Three-way valve
  • j. Four-way valve
  • k. Throttle (needle) valve
  • l. Pressure regulator

1.2 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for the following types of valve operators: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.vii

  • a. Diaphragm valve operator
  • b. Motor valve operator
  • c. Solenoid valve operator
  • d. Piston (hydraulic) valve operator
  • e. Hand (manual) valve operator
  • f. Reach-rod valve operator

1.3 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for educators and ejectors. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.vii

1.4 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for the following lines: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.vii

  • a. Process
  • b. Pneumatic
  • c. Hydraulic
  • d. Inert gas
  • e. Instrument signal (electrical)
  • f. Instrument capillary
  • g. Electrical

1.5 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for the following basic types of instrumentation: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.viii

  • a. Differential pressure cell
  • b. Temperature element
  • c. Venturi
  • d. Orifice
  • e. Rotometer
  • f. Conductivity or salinity cell
  • g. Radiation detector

1.6 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs to denote the location, either local or board mounted, of instruments, indicators, and controllers. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.viii

1.7 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for the following types of instrument signal controllers and modifiers: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.viii

  • a. Proportional
  • b. Proportional-integral
  • c. Proportional-integral-differential
  • d. Square root extractors

1.8 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering P&IDs for the following types of system components: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.viii

  • a. Centrifugal pumps
  • b. Positive displacement pumps
  • c. Heat exchangers
  • d. Compressors
  • e. Fans
  • f. Tanks
  • g. Filters/strainers

1.9 STATE how the following valve conditions are depicted on an engineering P&ID: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.ix

  • a. Open valve
  • b. Closed valve
  • c. Throttled valve
  • d. Combination valves (3- or 4-way valve)
  • e. Locked-closed valve
  • f. Locked-open valve
  • g. Fail-open valve
  • h. Fail-closed valve
  • i. Fail-as-is valve

1.10 Given an engineering P&ID, IDENTIFY components and DETERM INE the flowpath(s) for a given valve lineup. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.ix

1.11 IDENTIFY the symbols used on engineering fluid power drawings for the following components: DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.ix

  • a. Pump
  • b. Compressor
  • c. Reservoir
  • d. Actuators
  • e. Piping and piping junctions
  • f. Valves

1.12 Given a fluid power type drawing, DETERM INE the operation or resultant action of the stated component when hydraulic pressure is applied/removed. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.ix

Valve symbols

Objectives 1.1

"To read and interpret piping and instrument drawings (P&IDs), the reader must learn the meaning of the symbols." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.2
"The reader should note that this chapter is only representative of fluid system symbology, rather than being all-inclusive." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.2

Facility drafting standards give the symbols used at a site. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.2

"Valves are used to control the direction, flow rate, and pressure of fluids." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.3
"Figure 1 shows the symbols that depict the major valve types." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.3

Globe and gate valves will often be shown by the same symbol. The valve type may then be given by the component identification number or the notes and legend, but in many cases even those will not say. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.3

Knowledge check: Valve symbols

Objective 1.1Q1201

A P&ID shows a globe valve and a gate valve with the same symbol. Where might the valve type be given?

The answer is C. Information on the valve type may be conveyed by the component identification number or the notes and legend, though in many instances even that may not hold true. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.3

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1202

What are valves used to control?

The answer is D. Valves are used to control the direction, flow rate, and pressure of fluids. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.3

Valve actuators and control valves

Objectives 1.2

"Some valves are provided with actuators to allow remote operation, to increase mechanical advantage, or both." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4
"Figure 2 shows the symbols for the common valve actuators." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

Each actuator is shown on a gate valve, but an actuator can be attached to any type of valve body. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

"If no actuator is shown on a valve symbol, it may be assumed the valve is equipped only with a handwheel for manual operation." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4
"The combination of a valve and an actuator is commonly called a control valve." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

Control valves are shown by combining the valve symbol and the actuator symbol. Most are controlled manually from a remote station, automatically from an instrument, or both. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

Remote control often uses a small intermediate control valve in the line that supplies motive force to the process control valve. In this example, a solenoid-operated 3-way valve can supply air to the diaphragm or vent it to the atmosphere. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

The symbols alone do not show whether air pressure opens or closes the valve, or whether energizing the solenoid pressurizes or vents the diaphragm. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.5

"it does not provide enough information to determine how those components react to a control signal." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.5

A control valve run by an instrument is drawn the same way, except the output of the controlling instrument goes to the actuator. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.5

"An additional aspect of some control valves is a valve positioner, which allows more precise control of the valve." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.5
"A positioner is symbolized by a square box on the stem of the control valve actuator." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.5

The positioner symbol may appear only on detailed diagrams. Larger overall system diagrams may show the same valve as an air-operated valve with no special features. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.6

Knowledge check: Valve actuators and control valves

Objective 1.2Q1203

No actuator is shown on a valve symbol. What may be assumed?

The answer is A. If no actuator is shown on a valve symbol, it may be assumed the valve is equipped only with a handwheel for manual operation. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

Report a problem
Objective 1.2Q1204

On a P&ID valve actuator symbol, what does a box with the letter M mean?

The answer is A. Figure 2 shows a box marked M on the valve stem for an electric motor actuator. The box marked S is a solenoid. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

Report a problem
Objective 1.2Q1205

How is a valve positioner symbolized?

The answer is D. A positioner is symbolized by a square box on the stem of the control valve actuator. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.5

Report a problem
Objective 1.2Q1206

What is a control valve?

The answer is A. The combination of a valve and an actuator is commonly called a control valve. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.4

Report a problem

Control valve designations

Objectives 1.2

"To differentiate between valve uses, a balloon labeling system is used to identify the function of a control valve, as shown in Figure 6." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.6
"The common convention is that the first letter used in the valve designator indicates the parameter to be controlled by the valve." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.6
  • F = flow
  • T = temperature
  • L = level
  • P = pressure
  • H = hand (manually operated valve)

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.6

The second letter is usually a C, which identifies the valve as a controller, or active component. The third letter is a V, which shows the equipment is a valve. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.6

Piping and fitting symbols

Objectives 1.3, 1.4

One system's piping may carry more than one medium, and a fluid system diagram may also show instrument signals and electrical wires. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.7

"Figure 7 shows commonly used symbols for indicating the medium" DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.7

The auxiliary piping symbols identify their mediums, but the process flow line symbol does not. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.7

"Figure 8 shows symbols used to depict pipe fittings." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.8

Eductor and ejector symbols are both drawn in the line with a curved upper section and a nozzle shape below. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.8

Knowledge check: Piping and fitting symbols

Objective 1.4Q1208

On a P&ID line symbol, what do X marks along the line show?

The answer is A. Figure 7 shows X marks along the line for instrument capillary. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.7

Report a problem
Objective 1.4Q1209

On a P&ID line symbol, what do pairs of slashes along the line show?

The answer is A. Figure 7 shows pairs of slashes for a pneumatic (air) line. Single slashes mark an inert gas line. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.7

Report a problem
Objective 1.4Q1210

Which P&ID line symbol does not identify the medium it carries?

The answer is C. Although the auxiliary piping symbols identify their mediums, the symbol for the process flow line does not identify its medium. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.7

Instrument identifiers

Objectives 1.5

"One of the main purposes of a P&ID is to provide functional information about how instrumentation in a system or piece of equipment interfaces with the system or piece of equipment." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.8

Instrument symbols fall into four categories, and each generally uses the identifying scheme in Table 1. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.8

  • Sensed parameter: F flow, T temperature, P pressure, I current, L level, V voltage, Z position
  • Indicator or controller: R recorder, I indicator, C controller
  • Component: T transmitter, M modifier, E element
  • Signal: I current, V voltage, P pneumatic

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.9

"The first three columns above are combined such that the resulting instrument identifier indicates its sensed parameter, the function of the instrument, and the type of instrument." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.9

The fourth column is used only for a modifier, to show the signals being modified. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.9

  • FIC: flow indicating controller
  • TT: temperature transmitter
  • FM: flow modifier
  • PT: pressure transmitter
  • TE: temperature element
  • FE: flow element
  • TR: temperature recorder
  • LIC: level indicating controller

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.9

Modifiers, transmitters, and instrument location

Objectives 1.6

"Each sensor or detector must be coupled with appropriate modifiers and/or transmitters." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.11

The exceptions are certain local instruments with mechanical readouts, such as bourdon tube pressure gages and bimetallic thermometers. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.11

"Figure 10 also illustrates the common notations used to indicate the location of an instrument, i.e., local or board mounted." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.11

A transmitter converts the signal from a sensor or detector to a form that can be sent to a remote point. The output can be electronic (voltage or current), pneumatic, or hydraulic. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.11

A modifier may be identified only by its input and output signals, such as I/P for one that converts an electrical input to a pneumatic output, rather than by the monitored parameter, such as PM for pressure modifier. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.11

Indicators and recorders convert the signal from an instrument loop into a readable form. Like modifiers and transmitters, the symbol shows whether they are locally or board mounted. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.12

Controllers and signal conditioners

Objectives 1.7

"Controllers process the signal from an instrument loop and use it to position or manipulate some other system component." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.12

Controllers are generally shown by placing a C in the balloon after the controlling parameter. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.12

"Note that these types of controllers are also called signal conditioners." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.12

Figure 10 shows a square root extractor as a circle or square holding a square root sign. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.11

In Figure 14 (A), a temperature transmitter sends one signal to a board-mounted recorder and one to a PID controller. An I/P modifier converts the controller output to a pneumatic signal, commonly 3 psi to 15 psi, which operates the valve. The loop modifies flow based on process fluid temperature. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.13

In Figure 14 (B), a pneumatic level transmitter feeds a board-mounted level modifier, which drives a recorder and sends a modified pneumatic signal to the level control valve. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.13

Neither loop shows how the sensed value and the valve are related. Knowing the setpoint and the purpose of the system will usually be enough to work out how the loop operates. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.13

Valve status

Objectives 1.9

The reader must be able to determine the valve position, know if it is normal, know how the valve will fail, and in some cases know if it is normally locked in that position. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16

"Figure 17 illustrates the symbols used to indicate valve status." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16
  • Open valve: outlined, not filled
  • Closed valve: filled solid
  • Throttled valve: one half filled
  • Three-way valve: the closed port is filled
  • Locked open: LO; locked closed: LC
  • Fails open: FO; fails closed: FC; fails as is: FAI

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16

"Unless otherwise stated, P&IDs indicate valves in their "normal" position." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16

This is usually taken as the normal or primary flowpath for the system. Safety systems are the exception, and are normally shown in their standby or non-accident condition. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16

"3-way valves are sometimes drawn in the position that they will fail to instead of always being drawn in their "normal" position." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16

This will be defined as the standard for the system of drawings or noted on the drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16

Fluid power pumps and reservoirs

Objectives 1.11

Fluid power diagrams use a different set of symbols, though some match or resemble those on P&IDs. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23

"Fluid power includes either gas (such as air) or hydraulic (such as water or oil) motive media." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23
"Fluid power systems are divided into five basic parts: pumps, reservoirs, actuators, valves, and lines." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23

The basic pump symbol is a circle with one or more arrow heads showing the flow direction, with the points of the arrows touching the circle. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23

"Hydraulic pumps are shown by solid arrow heads." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23
"Pneumatic compressors are represented by hollow arrow heads." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23
"Reservoirs provide a location for storage of the motive media (hydraulic fluid or compressed gas)." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.24

Pneumatic reservoirs are usually simple tanks, drawn as a variation of a cylinder. Hydraulic reservoirs can be more complex, so their symbols show how fluid is admitted and removed. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.24

Fluid power actuators and lines

Objectives 1.11

"An actuator in a fluid power system is any device that converts the hydraulic or pneumatic pressure into mechanical work." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.24

Actuators are classified as linear or rotary. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.24

"Linear actuators have some form of piston device." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.24
"Rotary actuators are generally called motors and may be fixed or variable." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.25
"The difference between them is that the point of the arrow touches the circle in a pump and the tail of the arrow touches the circle in a motor." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.25
"The sole purpose of piping in a fluid power system is to transport the working media, at pressure, from one point to another." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.26

Fluid power valves

Objectives 1.11

"Valves are the most complicated symbols in fluid power systems." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.27

A fluid power valve commonly has three to eight pipes attached and can route one or more fluids in many combinations, so its symbol must hold more information than a standard P&ID valve. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.27

"Fluid power valves, when electrically operated by a solenoid, are drawn in the de-energized position." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.27
"Energizing the solenoid will cause the valve to shift to the other port." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.27

If the valve is operated by something other than a solenoid or is a multiport valve, the information needed will be on the drawing or its legend print. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.27

Reading a fluid power diagram

Objectives 1.12

Each part of a simple system can be listed with its symbol and redrawn as a fluid power diagram. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.30

First get an overall view. In this diagram, the arrows between A and B show the system presses or clamps a part between two sections of the machine. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.31

  • Area 1: open reservoir with a strainer that cleans the oil
  • Area 2: fixed displacement pump, electrically operated
  • Area 3: spring-operated relief valve with a separate pressure gage
  • Area 4: 4-way, 2-position valve, shown de-energized
  • Area 5: actuating cylinder and piston

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.32

"When system pressure exceeds its setpoint, the valve opens and returns the hydraulic fluid back to the reservoir." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.32

As drawn, high pressure fluid goes from Port 1 to Port 3 and to the bottom chamber, which holds the piston retracted. When the piston is fully retracted, the relief valve lifts and holds system pressure at setpoint. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.32

"When PB-1 is pushed and S-1 energized, the 1-2 ports are aligned and 3-4 ports are aligned." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.32

Fluid then enters the top chamber and drives the piston down, while the bottom chamber drains through ports 3-4 to the reservoir. The piston travels until PB-1 is released or full travel is reached. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.32

Types of fluid power diagrams

Objectives 1.12

"A pictorial diagram shows the physical arrangement of the elements in a system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.33

Pictorial diagrams show outlines of each item, not internal function, and are not especially valuable for maintenance or troubleshooting. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.33

"A cutaway diagram shows both the physical arrangement and the operation of the different components." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.33

Cutaway diagrams are generally used for instruction. They need so much space that they are not usually used for complicated systems. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.33

"A schematic diagram uses symbols to show the elements in a system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.34
"They do not accurately represent the relative location of the components." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.34

Schematics supply the functional information of the system, and are useful in maintenance and troubleshooting. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.34

Worked examples

Objective 1.10

Identify components on a P&ID

Using the exercise P&ID, identify a centrifugal pump, a heat exchanger, the tank, the venturi, the rupture disc, a relief valve, and the current-to-pneumatic converter.

  1. Pumps are drawn as circles with a tangent outlet: A and B.
  2. Heat exchangers are circles with a zigzag tube: C and D.
  3. The tank is E, the venturi is 31, and the rupture disc is 1.
  4. Relief valves are 8 and 17. The I/P box is 28.

Answer: Pump A or B, heat exchanger C or D, tank E, venturi 31, rupture disc 1, relief valve 8 or 17, converter 28.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.21

Objective 1.10

Read valve types and status

On the same P&ID, identify the motor-operated valves, the air-operated valves, the check valves, the solenoid valves, and the locked valves.

  1. A box marked M on the stem is a motor operator: 2, 3, 7, and 16.
  2. A dome on the stem is an air-operated diaphragm: 10 and 21.
  3. Check valves are 5 and 14. Solenoid valves are 11 and 23.
  4. Solid valves marked LC are locked closed: 18 and 19. Valve 4 is marked LO.

Answer: Motor 2, 3, 7, 16; air 10, 21; check 5, 14; solenoid 11, 23; locked closed 18, 19; locked open 4.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.21

Objective 1.10

Find the controlling parameter

What is the controlling parameter for Valves 10 and 21?

  1. Trace the signal back from each valve's diaphragm to the I/P modifier.
  2. Follow the dashed signal lines from the modifier to the elements marked TE.

Answer: Temperature, as sensed by the temperature elements (TE).

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.21

Objective 1.10

Set a valve lineup

Which valves must change position for Pump B to supply flow to only points G and H?

  1. Pump B must reach the upper train, so a closed cross-connect has to open.
  2. Flow to outlets F and I must be stopped at their outlet valves.

Answer: Open 18 and/or 19. Shut 13 and 25.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.21

Objective 1.10

Read the failure modes

Which valves fail open, fail closed, and fail as is?

  1. Look for the FO, FC, and FAI marks next to each valve.

Answer: Fail open: 2 and 3. Fail closed: 10 and 21. Fail as is: 7 and 16.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.21

Summary

  • This chapter reviewed the common P&ID symbols for valves, valve operators, process piping, instrumentation, and common system components. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.15
  • P&IDs show valves in their normal position unless otherwise stated, with symbols for valve condition and failure mode. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.16
  • Reading a P&ID means identifying the components, then working out the flowpath for a given valve lineup. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.18
  • Fluid power diagrams use their own symbols for pumps, reservoirs, actuators, valves, and lines. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.23
  • Pictorial, cutaway, and schematic diagrams all show fluid power systems, and schematics give the functional information. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-02 p.34
